strengths: The problem is well-motivated, timely, and sufficiently well-positioned in the literature
The proposed method appears straightforward to apply and seems to be effective in the proposed experiments
The paper is clearly written and organized
The paper tackles an interesting problem for the community: constrained Gaussian Processes. It effectively motivates the issue and includes substantial relevant related work.
The paper is well written and gives a good overview on the related work
The main (and perhaps only) strength of this paper is that it tackles a problem which I personally am interested in.
weaknesses: Limited descriptions, missing details: while the manuscript is well-written, it leaves many details of the proposed method to be filled in by the reader, making it difficult to judge its applicability in complex scenarios; it does not explicitly state any posteriors except for (3)-(4), hindering assessment of novelty and computational complexity; no details on the MCMC technique used, how constraints affect convergence, or why the restriction to GPs is important, requiring a more detailed discussion before its contribution can be judged.

Limited experimental validation: the applications are confined to low-dimensional settings with loose, linear constraints, failing to properly showcase performance or limitations; the constraint component is lax compared to the data component, and the impact of the ν parameter on behavior induction and numerical stability is unclear; the second application lacks parameter details and shows minimal effect of the constraint; missing comparisons to other baselines make it difficult to assess novelty.

Limited applicability: the proposed method penalizes constraint violations rather than enforcing them, so the resulting inference is not representative of the constrained Bayesian problem; there is insufficient theoretical and experimental validation to demonstrate the extent to which constraints are enforced; the method does not address the curse of dimensionality associated with virtual measurements.

Theoretical grounding and guarantees: the manuscript relies primarily on MCMC methods for inference but does not carefully examine relevant literature on penalties in MCMC, nor does it discuss assumptions underlying equations (3)-(4) and (5); it is unclear whether conditioning a GP on (5) is well-posed without strong assumptions on Φ, raising concerns about measurability and existence of the integral p(Φ | X, y).

The methods section lacks an in-depth analysis of the proposed method; there is no discussion about the resulting posterior, no presentation of an ELBO for variational inference, and the method's limitations and implications of different choices for Φ are not examined.

The experiments section is the weakest part of the paper; the authors do not compare their method with other relevant approaches, only against a heteroscedastic Gaussian Process, and should consider comparisons with approaches such as Riihimäki and Vehtari (2010).

It is challenging to identify the main contribution of this work; the authors claim a general framework for handling constraints but do not explore specific approaches to address posterior intractability, providing only an alternative perspective without clear benefits compared to previous tailored approaches.
The novelty compared to Hansen et al. and Riihimäki and Vehtari seems negligible; the authors do not argue improvements of their formulation of constraints compared to existing formulations.
The experiments only show qualitative results; there is not even one quantitative comparison in this paper.

The language used is very informal and not particularly appropriate for a paper; the introduction reads more like an informal conversation over coffee than an introduction trying to convince the reader of the importance of the problem.

There is no comparison to existing methods; without such comparisons it is unclear how the advantages/disadvantages of this work manifest in practice, whether it yields better approximations, when it is better or worse, or how its computational cost relates to competitors.

There is no discussion of ν; it is unclear why ν greater than zero would ever be taken, how to choose or estimate ν for applications, and what impact estimating ν has, especially given that exact function evaluations are feasible for linear Φ.

There is no discussion of limitations of this method; the paper omits mention of the additional cost of using virtual points, the computational cost of approximating the posterior, and details of the specific MCMC algorithm used, including its performance and speed.

The relevance of this paper to the ICLR community is questionable; the work may be more suitable for a workshop or a venue like AISTATS where the audience would be more aligned with this line of research.
